editorNote: The personal-computer market is no longer merely choosing machines; it is choosing standards. This week, IBM compatibility becomes the question hanging over every desk, while Coleco works to rescue Adam with restarted production and a promised library of familiar games.
morningLine: Good morning from 1984: the clones are gathering, Adam is back on the line, and Punch-Out!! is ringing the arcade bell.

lead.headline: IBM Compatibility Becomes the Industry’s New Battleground
lead.dek: An open hardware architecture, protected firmware and a vast software library turn “compatible” into the most valuable—and confusing—word in personal computing.
body: The flood of machines claiming kinship with the IBM Personal Computer has made compatibility one of the microcomputer trade’s most important and confusing questions. IBM published enough of the PC’s hardware design to invite expansion cards and outside development, but the machine’s basic input-output system remains copyrighted software. A look-alike case and an 8088-family processor alone do not make a true substitute.

For buyers, the test is practical. Will the machine boot the same operating system, run the same application programs, accept the same expansion cards and talk to the same printers and disks? Each “yes” gives a newcomer access to the broad catalog forming around the IBM standard. Each exception can turn a bargain into an island.

Clone builders therefore compete on more than price. Some promise portability, faster operation or more generous standard equipment; all must decide how closely to follow IBM without copying protected ROM code. Independently written firmware is becoming both an engineering achievement and a legal shield.

The result is a market reorganizing around software rather than badges. IBM created the reference machine, but a widening circle of compatible makers now wants the applications, dealers and customer confidence that surround it. The winner may be less a single computer than a common platform—provided shoppers learn exactly what each claim of compatibility means.

stories.headline: Coleco Restarts Adam Lines After a Gentleman’s C
body: Coleco resumed full Adam production at two upstate New York plants this week after a January inventory pause, returning its ambitious home computer to the line just as a prominent review assigned the machine an “A for ingenuity” but only a gentleman’s C for performance.

The roughly $600 package remains striking: a Z80A-based computer, keyboard, Digital Data Pack storage, daisy-wheel printer and ColecoVision cartridge compatibility in one box. Yet delayed deliveries and early reliability complaints have made dependable performance more urgent than the long feature list.

Restarting the factories can refill dealer shelves. Restoring confidence will require machines that work consistently—and enough worthwhile software to persuade families that Adam is more than a console with office ambitions.

stories.headline: “Best Of” Game Albums Promised for Adam
body: Coleco is courting established software publishers for “Best Of” collections intended to give Adam a faster route to a credible game catalog. Electronic Games Hotline led its February 12 issue with the plan, suggesting familiar titles could be assembled for the new machine rather than waiting for an entirely home-grown library.

The move recognizes the hard lesson of every new platform: specifications do not sell a computer for long without programs. Proven games could link Adam’s ColecoVision audience to its keyboard-and-printer future while buying developers time to create original software.

stories.headline: One Printer Attempts Double Duty
body: A new American printer reviewed this week tackles a familiar home-office compromise. Daisy-wheel machines make typewriter-crisp letters but offer little graphic freedom; dot-matrix printers draw charts and illustrations but often leave correspondence looking unmistakably computerized.

The attempt to bridge those jobs shows why the printer can be the most consequential accessory in a home system. A computer that calculates, writes and draws still needs one machine able to put all three kinds of work convincingly on paper.
